notes.text: Here is the trial of Abraham's faith, whether it continued so strong, so vigourous, so victorious, after a long settlement in communion with God, as it was at first, when by it he left his country: then it appeared that he loved God better than his father; now, that he loved him better than his son. After these things — After all the other exercises he had had, all the difficulties he had gone through: now perhaps he was beginning to think the storms were blown over but after all, this encounter comes, which is stranger than any yet. God did tempt Abraham - Not to draw him to sin, so Satan tempts; but to discover his graces, how strong they were, that they might be found to praise and honour and glory. The trial itself: God appeared to him as he had formerly done, called him by name Abraham, that name which had been given him in ratification of the promise: Abraham, like a good servant, readily answered, Here am I; what saith my Lord unto his servant? Probably he expected some renewed promise, like those, chap. xv, 1; xvii, 1, but to his great amazement that which God hath to say to him is in short, Abraham, go kill thy son: and this command is given him in such aggravating language as makes the temptation abundantly more grievous. When God speaks, Abraham, no doubt, takes notice of every word, and listens attentively to it: and every word here is a sword in his bones; the trial is steel'd with trying phrases. Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that he should afflict? No, it is not; yet when Abraham's faith is to be tried, God seems to take pleasure in the aggravation of the trial.

And he said, take thy son — Not thy bullocks and thy lambs; how willingly would Abraham have parted with them by thousands to redeem Isaac! Not thy servant, no, not the steward of thine house. Thine only son - Thine only son by Sarah. Ishmael was lately cast out, to the grief of Abraham, and now Isaac only was left and must he go too? Yes: take Isaac, him by name, thy laughter, that son indeed. Yea, that son whom thou lovest - The trial was of Abraham's love to God, and therefore it must be in a beloved son: in the Hebrew 'tis expressed more emphatically, and I think might very well be read thus, Take now that son of thine, that only son of thine, whom thou lovest, that Isaac. And get thee into the land of Moriah - Three days journey off: so that he might have time to consider it, and if he do it, must do it deliberately. And offer him for a burnt offering - He must not only kill his son, but kill him as a sacrifice, with all that sedateness and composedness of mind, with which he used to offer his burnt- offering.

The several steps of this obedience, all help to magnify it, and to shew that he was guided by prudence, and governed by faith, in the whole transaction. (1.) He rises early — Probably the command was given in the visions of the night, and early the next morning he sets himself about it, did not delay, did not demur. Those that do the will of God heartily will do it speedily. (2.) He gets things ready for a sacrifice, and it should seem, with his own hands, cleaves the wood for the burnt-offering. (3.) He left his servants at some distance off, left they should have created him some disturbance in his strange oblation. Thus when Christ was entering upon his agony in the garden, he took only three of his disciples with him.
Isaac's carrying the wood was a type of Christ, who carried his own cross, while Abraham, with a steady and undaunted resolution, carried the fatal knife and fire.

Behold the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb? — This is,

1. A trying question to Abraham; how could he endure to think that Isaac is himself the lamb?

2. 'Tis a teaching question to us all, that when we are going to worship God, we should seriously consider whether we have every thing ready, especially the lamb for a burnt-offering. Behold, the fire is ready; that is, the Spirit's assistance, and God's acceptance: the wood is ready, the instituted ordinances designed to kindle our affections, which indeed, without the Spirit, are but like wood without fire, but the Spirit works by them. All things are now ready, but where is the lamb? Where is the heart? Is that ready to be offered up to God, to ascend to him as a burnt- offering?

My son, God will provide himself a lamb — This was the language either,

1. Of his obedience; we must offer the lamb which God has appointed now to be offered; thus giving him this general rule of submission to the divine will to prepare him for the application of it to himself. Or,

2. Of his faith; whether he meant it so or no, this proved to be the meaning of it; a sacrifice was provided instead of Isaac. Thus,

1. Christ the great sacrifice of atonement was of God's providing: when none in heaven or earth could have found a lamb for that burnt-offering, God himself found the ransom.

2. All our sacrifices of acknowledgement are of God's providing too; 'tis he that prepares the heart. The broken and contrite spirit is a sacrifice of God, of his providing.

9. With the same resolution and composedness of mind, he applies himself to the compleating of this sacrifice. After many a weary step, and with a heavy heart, he arrives at length at the fatal place; builds the altar, an altar of earth, we may suppose, the saddest that ever be built; lays the wood in order for Isaac's funeral pile; and now tells him the amazing news. Isaac, for ought appears, is as willing as Abraham; we do not find that he made any objection against it. God commands it to be done, and Isaac has learned to submit. Yet it is necessary that a sacrifice be bound; the great Sacrifice, which, in the fulness of time, was to be offered up, must be bound, and therefore so must Isaac. Having bound him he lays him upon the altar, and his hand upon the head of the sacrifice. Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and wonder, O earth! here is an act of faith and obedience which deserves to be a spectacle to God, angels and men; Abraham's darling, the church's hope, the heir of promise, lies ready to bleed and die by his own father's hands! Now this obedience of Abraham in offering up Isaac is a lively representation,

1. Of the love of God to us, in delivering up his only begotten Son to suffer and die for us, as a sacrifice. Abraham was obliged both in duty and gratitude to part with Isaac and parted with him to a friend, but God was under no obligations to us, for we were enemies.

2. Of our duty to God in return of that love we must tread in the steps of this faith of Abraham. God, by his word, calls us to part with all for Christ, all our sins, tho' they have been as a right hand, or a right eye, or an Isaac; all those things that are rivals with Christ for the sovereignity of our heart; and we must cheerfully let them all go. God, by his providence, which is truly the voice of God, calls us to part with an Isaac sometimes, and we must do it by a chearful resignation and submission to his holy will.
The Angel of the Lord — That is, God himself, the eternal Word, the Angel of the covenant, who was to be the great Redeemer and Comforter.

Lay not thine hand upon the lad — God's time to help his people is, when they are brought to the greatest extremity: the more eminent the danger is, and the nearer to be put in execution, the more wonderful and the more welcome is the deliverance. Now know I that thou fearest God - God knew it before, but now Abraham had given a memorable evidence of it. He need do no more, what he had done was sufficient to prove the religious regard he had to God and his authority. The best evidence of our fearing God is our being willing to honour him with that which is dearest to us, and to part with all to him, or for him.

Behold a ram — Tho' that blessed Seed was now typified by Isaac, yet the offering of him up was suspended 'till the latter end of the world, and in the mean time the sacrifice of beasts was accepted, as a pledge of that expiation which should be made by that great sacrifice. And it is observable, that the temple, the place of sacrifice, was afterward built upon this mount Moriah, 2 Chron. iii, 1, and mount Calvary, where Christ was crucified, was not far off.

And Abraham called the place Jehovah-jireh — The Lord will provide. Probably alluding to what he had said, ver. 8. God will provide himself a lamb - This was purely the Lord's doing: let it be recorded for the generations to come; that the Lord will see; he will always have his eyes upon his people in their straits, that he may come in with seasonable succor in the critical juncture. And that he will be seen, be seen in the mount, in the greatest perplexities of his people; he will not only manifest but magnify his wisdom, power and goodness in their deliverance. Where God sees and provides, he should be seen and praised. And perhaps it may refer to God manifest in the flesh.

glossa.text: « Which things after they were done, » etc. ((AUG., Quaest. in Gen., tom. III.)) James says that God tempts no man; but in ordinary usage we say "to tempt" for that which is "to prove". James however speaks of that temptation by which every man is entangled in sin [ *Al.,* peccator]. Whence I Thess. I: « Lest perhaps he that tempteth should have tempted you. » For elsewhere it is written Deut. XIII: « Your God tempteth you, that he may know whether you love him, that is, that he may make you to know. » For a man knows not the powers of his own love, unless he learns it by experience.

« Take thy son, » etc. ((ALC. in Gen., tom. I.)) Abraham was not bidden to kill his son at once, but to lead him for three days to the sacrifice, that by the length of the time the temptation might be increased. For through three days, with cares increasing, a father's bowels are tormented, and for a long space the father gazes upon his son, takes food with him, so many nights the boy hangs in his father's embrace, lies in his lap, and at every moment the grief of killing his son is heaped up in a father's love.

« Whom thou lovest, » etc. ((BEDA in Gen., c. 22.)) By the reminder of love and the recalling of the name the temptation is heaped up, and a father's affection is stirred at the memory of the promise, because it was said: « In Isaac shall thy seed be called, » as though, if he were killed, the whole hope of the promise would be frustrated.

« Go into the land. » ((HIER. Q. Hebr., tom. III.)) The Hebrews say that this mountain is that in which the temple was afterwards built, on the threshing-floor of Orna the Jebusite. Whence II, Par. III: « They began to build the temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, in mount Moria, » which is for that cause interpreted *illuminating* and *shining,* because there is *debir* ( ) that is, the oracle of God, and the Spirit who teaches men the truth and inspires prophecies.
« Leading his ass, » etc. ((ISID. in Gen., c. 18.)) The ass signifies the senseless folly of the Jews, which bore all the sacraments and knew them not.

« And on the third day. » ((HIER. ubi supra.)) It is to be noted that from Gerara as far as mount Moria, that is, the seat of the temple, is a journey of three days: and Abraham is said to have arrived there on the third day. Wrongly therefore do they think that Abraham dwelt at that time by the oak of Mambre, since to mount Moria there is scarce a full day's journey. The three days in which they came to the place of the sacrifice signify three ages, before the law, from Abraham to Moses; under the law, from Moses to John; thence to the Lord; and whatever remains, the third day is that of grace, in which third age the sacrifice of Christ was completed.

« Stay here, » etc. ((ISID. ubi supra.)) Hear the Apostle: « Blindness in part happeneth in Israel, » that is, « with the ass, » that « the fulness of the Gentiles might come in, » that is, « after we have adored. » When the sacrifice of the cross shall have been preached among the Gentiles, that is, « when the fulness of the Gentiles shall have come in, we will return to you, » that is, « and so all Israel shall be saved. » The two servants left behind, and not brought to the place of the sacrifice, are the Jews who, living slavishly and savouring carnally, understood not the humility and passion of Christ. Two indeed, because they were to be divided into two parts, which came to pass when Solomon sinned, when the people was divided in respect of the kingdom, not by the error of impiety, to whom it is said Jer. III: « Israel the adversary, and Juda the prevaricator. » 

« I and the boy, » etc. ((ALC.)) With undoubting mind he willed to slay his son. He is to be praised in the constancy of offering and in the faith of raising up. For he knew most certainly that God cannot deceive, and that, though the boy were killed, yet the promise of God would remain safe. Whence the Apostle Hebr. XI: « By faith Abraham hesitated not, when he offered up his only-begotten, in whom he had received the promise, believing that God is able to raise up even from the dead. » 

« Abraham said. » ((ISID. ubi supra.)) Abraham, leading his only son to be sacrificed, signifies God the Father. Abraham received a son in old age, but God grows not old, yet the promise concerning Christ had in a manner grown old when he was born. It began from Adam, when it was said: « They shall be two in one flesh » ((Gen. II)); and it was completed in the sixth age of the world. Sara's old age in the people of God, that is, in the multitude of the prophets, signifies this same thing, because in the end of the times Christ was born of the people of holy souls. Her barrenness signifies that in this world we are saved by hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we are all born, which birth of the Church [ *Al.,* Ecclesia] in the end of the times not nature but grace brought forth. Abraham therefore signifies God the Father, Isaac Christ. For as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so God the Father delivered up his only-begotten Son for us. And as Isaac carried the wood upon which he was to be laid, so Christ the cross on which he was to be fastened.

« And when he had bound, » etc. ((ISID. ubi supra.)) Isaac with his feet bound is laid upon the altar, and Christ is fastened to the cross. But that which was figured by Isaac was transferred to the ram, because Christ is a sheep. For he is a son, because born; a ram, because sacrificed. The ram sticks fast in the briars, the cross has horns. For if two pieces of wood be joined together, the shape of a cross is produced. Whence Habac. III: « Horns in his hands. » The ram therefore sticking fast by the horns is Christ crucified. But briars are thorns: wicked thorns, which hanged the Lord. For among the thorns of sinners he was hanged. Whence Jer.: « With the thorns of their sins this people hath encompassed me ((Jer. XXXVIII.)) » Others understand this ram bound in the briars to be Christ crowned with thorns before his immolation.

« Thou hast not spared, » etc. ((AUG. ubi supra.)) Did Abraham then not spare his son on account of the angel? But in the angel the Lord was figured, who is God and the angel of great counsel. For God was in the angel, and spoke in his person. This will appear the more in what follows, when it is said: « And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord. » For it is not easily found that Christ calls the Father Lord, especially before the incarnation. For according to the flesh this is congruously said, according to which it is said in the second psalm: « The Lord said to me, » etc. But that which is said in the same place, c. 9: « The Lord said to my Lord, » etc., is referred to the prophet who speaks; as that: « The Lord rained from the Lord, » that is, our Lord, namely the Son, from our Lord, namely the Father.

« The ram. » *((ALC.)) Historically.* The ram which was sacrificed for Isaac, we have not imagined [it], but it is true. Therefore it is rather thought that an angel brought it from elsewhere, than that the Lord created it there out of the earth after the work of the six days.

« The ram among the briars, » etc. ((HIER. in Quaest. Hebr.)) Aquila put *a briar* or *a thorn-brake,* etc., *as far as* which is so said in Hebrew.
« And he called the name, » etc. ((HIER. ubi supra.)) For that which is had here, etc., *as far as* namely through the incarnation.

notes.text: How long — Shall I be in such perplexities, not knowing what course to take?
Lighten — Revive and comfort, and deliver me from the darkness of death, which is ready to come upon me.

I will sing — It is a common thing for David and other prophets to speak of future deliverances as if they were already come, that so they may signify both the infallible certainty of the thing, and their firm assurance thereof. The atheism and corruption of mankind, ver. 1-3. An expostulation with sinners, ver. 4-6. A prayer for the salvation of God, ver. 7. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*How long.* ((CAS.)) Great is the ardour of him who endures, etc., *as far as* because hope is drawn out.

*Counsels.* ((AUG.)) There is no need of counsel, etc., *as far as* grieving and praying for eternal things.

*How long shall he be exalted,* etc. ((CASS.)) He says that before the coming of Christ the devil held men captive. Or *over me,* that is, over my cruelty, because he is worshipped in the whole world; and because the world so perishes, he weeps.

*Look thou upon me. ((Ibid.))* After the complaint, a prayer, that he may be enlightened, lest he yield to the frauds of the enemy, he who trusts in mercy. *Look thou upon me.* ((AUG.)) Send him whom thou art to send. *Hear me.* ((CASS.)) For all, for whom he asks in general. *Enlighten.* If not in body, let us see at least in mind. *That I sleep.* When, the light of faith being buried, they are shut up in carnal delight. *In death.* That is, in the sin which is committed against the Holy Spirit, of which John says: *There is a sin unto death, I do not say for it that any man should pray.*

*They shall rejoice.* ((AUG.)) Not only for enlightening me, but lest the enemy rejoice. *I have hoped* ((CASS.)) And though he makes haste, yet he is patient: because even if it is put off, he is firm in hope, and already seeing inwardly he exults over him whom he longs to see in the flesh: whence he who before complained says that good things have already been given him. *He hath given.* Not, he will give: the great power of faith already has what is to come. *My heart shall rejoice.* If he desires so much, if he so serves him who is to come, what must be done when he has been received?

notes.text: Let not sin reign even in your mortal body — It must be subject to death, but it need not be subject to sin.
Neither present your members to sin — To corrupt nature, a mere tyrant. But to God - Your lawful King.

Sin shall not have dominion over you — It has neither right nor power. For ye are not under the law - A dispensation of terror and bondage, which only shows sin, without enabling you to conquer it. But under grace - Under the merciful dispensation of the gospel, which brings complete victory over it to every one who is under the powerful influences of the Spirit of Christ.

The form of doctrine into which ye have been delivered — Literally it is, The mould into which ye have been delivered; which, as it contains a beautiful allusion, conveys also a very instructive admonition; intimating that our minds, all pliant and ductile, should be conformed to the gospel precepts, as liquid metal, take the figure of the mould into which they are cast.

Being then set free from sin — We may see the apostles method thus far at one view: - Chap. Ver.

1. Bondage to sin chap. iii, 9

2. The knowledge of sin by the law; a sense of God's wrath; inward death chap. iii, 20

3. The Revelation of the righteousness of God in Christ through the gospel chap. iii, 21

4. The center of all, faith, embracing that righteousness chap. iii, 22

5. Justification, whereby God forgives all past sin, and freely accepts the sinner chap. iii, 24

6. The gift of the Holy Ghost; a sense of chap. v, 5, God's love new inward life ver. 4

7. The free service of righteousness ver. 12

I speak after the manner of men — Thus it is necessary that the scripture should let itself down to the language of men. Because of the weakness of your flesh - Slowness of understanding flows from the weakness of the flesh, that is, of human nature. As ye have presented your members servants to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members servants of righteousness unto holiness - Iniquity (whereof uncleanness is an eminent part) is here opposed to righteousness; and unto iniquity is the opposite of unto holiness. Righteousness here is a conformity to the divine will; holiness, to the whole divine nature. Observe, they who are servants of righteousness go on to holiness; but they who are servants to iniquity get no farther. Righteousness is service, because we live according to the will of another; but liberty, because of our inclination to it, and delight in it.

When ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness — In all reason, therefore, ye ought now to be free from unrighteousness; to be as uniform and zealous in serving God as ye were in serving the devil.
Those things — He speaks of them as afar off.

Death — Temporal, spiritual, and eternal. Is the due wages of sin; but eternal life is the gift of God - The difference is remarkable. Evil works merit the reward they receive: good works do not. The former demand wages: the latter accept a free gift.

glossa.text:
*Let it not therefore.* Because above he said that we are dead to sins, and ought not to live in it, since no one is without sin: he determines what things are most of all to be guarded against, as though he concluded what was asked above: Shall we continue in sin.

*That you should obey its concupiscences.* Concupiscence is sometimes a name for the *fomes*, namely for the inborn vice; sometimes for the inward act, which is present both in the first motion, which is called *propassio*, and in the second, which is called delight, and in the third, which is called consent. Here he does not forbid the concupiscence that is in the first motion, because it is not in our power when it rises: but by the grace of God we can restrain it, that it may not come as far as delight and consent, which he does forbid.

*What then?* Because the law is from God, he sins who forsakes it for grace. *What then? Shall we sin.* Because we are not under the law, which terrifies, but under grace, which promises well? what then? shall we sin? This certain men [say], who preach that the law is, as it were, cleaving to us or coercing us, and is to be held to.
*Know you not that,* etc. Lest, professing God in words, we should be made the devil's, he forewarns us that we are the servants of him whose will we do.

*But thanks be to God,* etc. He both shows their change, and has disclosed how pleasing this is to him, offering a hymn to God. For you were, he says, the servants of sin: but of your own accord and by the free will of your mind you shook off his dominion, and embraced the spiritual doctrine. *The form of doctrine.* Our doctrine is a form, which restores the deformed image of God.

*A human thing,* etc. Thus far the Apostle has shown that one must not sin. Here he says what is to be done thenceforward, namely that justice be served, concerning which there is no one who can excuse himself, because there is no one who cannot work well, at least in will: which is the same thing through grace.

*For as you have yielded,* etc. ((AUG.)) If not more, at least as much as then, lest the faith should be shunned as harsh and insupportable.

As then no fear compelled, but the lust and pleasure of sin led, so now the delight of a justice grown up leads, though not yet perfect; whence he said: *A human thing.*

*So now.* Because justice ought even to be loved more than iniquity then was, so that for justice a man may bear pains, and despise all things, even death.

*Free.* It is the servant's liberty when it delights him to sin, which comes of free choice. He serves freely who gladly does the will of the Lord; and so he serves justice freely who loves, who rejoices.

*What fruit therefore.* This recalling makes former things abhorrent, and makes us the more beholden to grace. *You are ashamed.* For there is a certain temporal confusion, namely a disturbance of the mind looking back upon its own sins, and shuddering at the sight, and blushing at the shudder, and correcting itself by the blush. *The end of them,* etc. Because death is the worthy recompense for sin: but eternal life, which is the end of the just, is given by grace alone through Christ, because both the merits are from grace, and grace will be rendered for grace.

*But now being made free. ((AUG.))* He said *free* with respect to justice, not *made free*: now, with respect to sin, not *free*, lest they ascribe this to themselves, but he accordingly says *made free*, according to the sentence of the Lord: *If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed ((Joan. VIII))*.

*The wages.* Rightly a wage, because to the devil's warfare eternal death is rendered as a debt. To whom would the just Judge render a crown, if the merciful Father had not bestowed grace? how would that debt be rendered, unless that grace were first freely bestowed?

((AUG.)) Since sins had far separated the human race from God, we had to be reconciled through a mediator, who alone was born without sin, lived and was slain, so that human pride might both be reproved and healed through the humility of God, and it might be shown to man how far he had withdrawn from God, etc.

notes.text: Matt. xviii, 5; Luke x, 16; John xiii, 20.
He that entertaineth a prophet — That is, a preacher of the Gospel: In the name of a prophet - That is, because he is such, shall share in his reward.
One of these little ones — The very least Christian. Mark ix, 41.

glossa.text: *He that receiveth,* etc. When he sends them to preach, etc., *as far as* that they ought to receive their wages.

*And whosoever.* He who by the testimony of the shaken-off dust denounced the peril of those who do not receive them, commends beyond what was hoped the desert of those who do receive them. Note that God looks rather to the devout affection than to the quantity of the thing bestowed. *To one of these least ones.* The least are those who have absolutely nothing in this world, and will be judges with Christ.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A type of death-and-resurrection-to-life that early Christian reading connected to Christ's raising; resonates with 6:4-5,8-9 union in death and resurrection. Faint and contested.

echoes.text: For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
echoes.note: 'For they are my servants (slaves), whom I brought out of the land of Egypt' (cf. 25:55). The structural logic of 6:16-22 - one cannot be masterless; freed from one slavery you become a slave of another, and God's people are rightly God's slaves - mirrors the exodus principle that liberation from Pharaoh = transfer to YHWH's service. Coheres with Paul's 'made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness/God.'

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: The two ways: 'I have set before you life and death... therefore choose life.' Romans 6:21-23 frames the alternatives as 'the end of those things is death' versus 'eternal life,' the same life-or-death covenantal antithesis. Thematic coherence is high even without verbatim borrowing.

glossa.text: *All the vessels,* etc. Jeremias had said that the remaining vessels also were to be carried away, this man affirms that those carried away are to be brought back.
*Amen, so,* etc. He wishes that to be done which the other has falsely said, etc., *as far as* under the example of others he asserts the truth.
*Nevertheless.* He could have said, thou liest, etc., *as far as* that they who hear may await the outcome.

notes.text: Sing — He prefaces this, lest the following complainers of present miseries should argue ingratitude for former mercies. Faithfulness - Whatsoever hath befallen us, it proceeded not from thy unfaithfulness.
Establish — As firmly and durably as the heavens themselves.
Chosen — With David; whom I have chosen to the kingdom.
Build up — I will perpetuate the kingdom to thy posterity; which was promised upon condition, and was literally accomplished in Christ.
Know — Who enjoy the presence of God and his ordinances, to which they are called by the sound of trumpets. Walk - Under the comfortable influences of thy favour.
Name — In the knowledge and remembrance of thy name, of thy infinite power and goodness.
The glory — To thee alone belongs the glory of all their valiant achievements.

glossa.text:
*The mercies.* ((CASS.)) This Psalm says many things concerning the hope of Christians and the magnificence of the Lord, by which no one is led astray who prays worthily, which the true Israel so understands. First the Prophet promises that he will sing of mercy and truth.

*For ever.* ((CASS., REM.)) How does he *sing the mercies for ever,* and give thanks, who is not mindful of misery? And how is there full blessedness if the memory of guilt touches the mind? But we often remember sad things in gladness, and sorrows in health without sorrow, and thence we are the more glad and thankful; and so likewise the recollection of misery takes away nothing of blessedness.

*Truth.* The promise. In the mouth: it does not slip out of the mouth, but is turned over long in the mouth as something sweet.

*For thou hast said.* Here he says: Whence does he know? and what are the mercies of God through Christ? ((AUG.)) Which mercies, and what truth shall I sing? Behold.

*For thou hast said.* As if he should say: I, a man, say securely what thou, God, hast said, hast made manifest through the Spirit.

*Mercy shall be built up.* ((AUG.)) He repeats both, which he foretold. Because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Truth is not shown forth in the fulfilling of the things promised, unless mercy go before in the remission of sins. Finally, truth pertains to the Jews, to whom the promises were made, mercy to the Gentiles: as the Apostle says: *For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, which was to be fulfilled: but that the Gentiles honour God for his mercy ((Rom. XV))* .

*In the heavens.* They who declare the glory of God, through whom mercy is built up .

*I have sworn to David my servant.* This man is secure, for this reason, because God has said it: more secure, because he has sworn. God's swearing is the confirmation of the promise, and out of both is made the man Ethan, that is, the strong one.

*For ever.* ((CASS.)) The building up of mercy is not temporal, as the ruin of iniquity is temporal: for temporal iniquity is destroyed in certain men, that in them eternal mercy may be built up, whence the Lord says to Jeremiah: *Behold therefore I have set thee over the nations and over kingdoms, to root up, and to pull down, and to waste, and to destroy, and to build, and to plant. Unto generation.* ((AUG.)) For generation cannot, etc., *as far as* he shall sit, and then in the saints.

*Blessed is the people that knoweth,* etc. ((CASS.)) He knows, who places his gladness not in his own strength, but in the Lord's, or, who understands in the heart what he sings with the mouth: whence this reward follows, *in the light,* that is, they shall persevere in the contemplation of the Trinity.

*Jubilation.* Jubilation is a joy which cannot be unfolded in words, nor yet altogether kept silent. *O Lord, they shall walk in the light of thy countenance, and in thy name they shall rejoice.* ((CASS.)) He commends the grace, of which the jubilation is.

((AUG.)) Or in thy good pleasure, that is, in Christ, therefore in him, because he took our flesh, in whom is all hope.

notes.text: Let not sin reign even in your mortal body — It must be subject to death, but it need not be subject to sin.
Neither present your members to sin — To corrupt nature, a mere tyrant. But to God - Your lawful King.

Sin shall not have dominion over you — It has neither right nor power. For ye are not under the law - A dispensation of terror and bondage, which only shows sin, without enabling you to conquer it. But under grace - Under the merciful dispensation of the gospel, which brings complete victory over it to every one who is under the powerful influences of the Spirit of Christ.

The form of doctrine into which ye have been delivered — Literally it is, The mould into which ye have been delivered; which, as it contains a beautiful allusion, conveys also a very instructive admonition; intimating that our minds, all pliant and ductile, should be conformed to the gospel precepts, as liquid metal, take the figure of the mould into which they are cast.

Being then set free from sin — We may see the apostles method thus far at one view: - Chap. Ver.

1. Bondage to sin chap. iii, 9

2. The knowledge of sin by the law; a sense of God's wrath; inward death chap. iii, 20

3. The Revelation of the righteousness of God in Christ through the gospel chap. iii, 21

4. The center of all, faith, embracing that righteousness chap. iii, 22

5. Justification, whereby God forgives all past sin, and freely accepts the sinner chap. iii, 24

6. The gift of the Holy Ghost; a sense of chap. v, 5, God's love new inward life ver. 4

7. The free service of righteousness ver. 12

I speak after the manner of men — Thus it is necessary that the scripture should let itself down to the language of men. Because of the weakness of your flesh - Slowness of understanding flows from the weakness of the flesh, that is, of human nature. As ye have presented your members servants to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members servants of righteousness unto holiness - Iniquity (whereof uncleanness is an eminent part) is here opposed to righteousness; and unto iniquity is the opposite of unto holiness. Righteousness here is a conformity to the divine will; holiness, to the whole divine nature. Observe, they who are servants of righteousness go on to holiness; but they who are servants to iniquity get no farther. Righteousness is service, because we live according to the will of another; but liberty, because of our inclination to it, and delight in it.

When ye were the servants of sin, ye were free from righteousness — In all reason, therefore, ye ought now to be free from unrighteousness; to be as uniform and zealous in serving God as ye were in serving the devil.
Those things — He speaks of them as afar off.

Death — Temporal, spiritual, and eternal. Is the due wages of sin; but eternal life is the gift of God - The difference is remarkable. Evil works merit the reward they receive: good works do not. The former demand wages: the latter accept a free gift.

glossa.text:
*Let it not therefore.* Because above he said that we are dead to sins, and ought not to live in it, since no one is without sin: he determines what things are most of all to be guarded against, as though he concluded what was asked above: Shall we continue in sin.

*That you should obey its concupiscences.* Concupiscence is sometimes a name for the *fomes*, namely for the inborn vice; sometimes for the inward act, which is present both in the first motion, which is called *propassio*, and in the second, which is called delight, and in the third, which is called consent. Here he does not forbid the concupiscence that is in the first motion, because it is not in our power when it rises: but by the grace of God we can restrain it, that it may not come as far as delight and consent, which he does forbid.

*What then?* Because the law is from God, he sins who forsakes it for grace. *What then? Shall we sin.* Because we are not under the law, which terrifies, but under grace, which promises well? what then? shall we sin? This certain men [say], who preach that the law is, as it were, cleaving to us or coercing us, and is to be held to.
*Know you not that,* etc. Lest, professing God in words, we should be made the devil's, he forewarns us that we are the servants of him whose will we do.

*But thanks be to God,* etc. He both shows their change, and has disclosed how pleasing this is to him, offering a hymn to God. For you were, he says, the servants of sin: but of your own accord and by the free will of your mind you shook off his dominion, and embraced the spiritual doctrine. *The form of doctrine.* Our doctrine is a form, which restores the deformed image of God.

*A human thing,* etc. Thus far the Apostle has shown that one must not sin. Here he says what is to be done thenceforward, namely that justice be served, concerning which there is no one who can excuse himself, because there is no one who cannot work well, at least in will: which is the same thing through grace.

*For as you have yielded,* etc. ((AUG.)) If not more, at least as much as then, lest the faith should be shunned as harsh and insupportable.

As then no fear compelled, but the lust and pleasure of sin led, so now the delight of a justice grown up leads, though not yet perfect; whence he said: *A human thing.*

*So now.* Because justice ought even to be loved more than iniquity then was, so that for justice a man may bear pains, and despise all things, even death.

*Free.* It is the servant's liberty when it delights him to sin, which comes of free choice. He serves freely who gladly does the will of the Lord; and so he serves justice freely who loves, who rejoices.

*What fruit therefore.* This recalling makes former things abhorrent, and makes us the more beholden to grace. *You are ashamed.* For there is a certain temporal confusion, namely a disturbance of the mind looking back upon its own sins, and shuddering at the sight, and blushing at the shudder, and correcting itself by the blush. *The end of them,* etc. Because death is the worthy recompense for sin: but eternal life, which is the end of the just, is given by grace alone through Christ, because both the merits are from grace, and grace will be rendered for grace.

*But now being made free. ((AUG.))* He said *free* with respect to justice, not *made free*: now, with respect to sin, not *free*, lest they ascribe this to themselves, but he accordingly says *made free*, according to the sentence of the Lord: *If the Son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed ((Joan. VIII))*.

*The wages.* Rightly a wage, because to the devil's warfare eternal death is rendered as a debt. To whom would the just Judge render a crown, if the merciful Father had not bestowed grace? how would that debt be rendered, unless that grace were first freely bestowed?

((AUG.)) Since sins had far separated the human race from God, we had to be reconciled through a mediator, who alone was born without sin, lived and was slain, so that human pride might both be reproved and healed through the humility of God, and it might be shown to man how far he had withdrawn from God, etc.

notes.text: Matt. xviii, 5; Luke x, 16; John xiii, 20.
He that entertaineth a prophet — That is, a preacher of the Gospel: In the name of a prophet - That is, because he is such, shall share in his reward.
One of these little ones — The very least Christian. Mark ix, 41.

glossa.text: *He that receiveth,* etc. When he sends them to preach, etc., *as far as* that they ought to receive their wages.

*And whosoever.* He who by the testimony of the shaken-off dust denounced the peril of those who do not receive them, commends beyond what was hoped the desert of those who do receive them. Note that God looks rather to the devout affection than to the quantity of the thing bestowed. *To one of these least ones.* The least are those who have absolutely nothing in this world, and will be judges with Christ.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]

echoes.text: It fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where there was a prominent woman; and she persuaded him to eat bread. So it was, that as often as he passed by, he turned in there to eat bread. She said to her husband, “See now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God, that passes by us continually. Please let us make a little room on the wall. Let us set for him there a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp stand. It shall be, when he comes to us, that he […]
echoes.note: The Shunammite woman receives Elisha, builds him a room, and is rewarded with a son and his resurrection. Together with the Zarephath account this supplies the OT pattern that receiving a prophet yields a prophet's reward (10:41).

echoes.text: A man from Baal Shalishah came, and brought the man of God bread of the first fruits, twenty loaves of barley, and fresh ears of grain in his sack. He said, “Give to the people, that they may eat.” His servant said, “What, should I set this before a hundred men?” But he said, “Give the people, that they may eat; for thus says Yahweh, ‘They will eat, and will have some left over.’” So he set it before them, and they ate, and left some of it, according to […]
echoes.note: The man who brings provisions to Elisha and 'the servant of the prophet' setting it before the people — a faint analogue to ministering to God's agents and not losing one's reward (10:42), within the same Elisha hospitality cycle.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: Giving the thirsty water to drink as a rewarded act of mercy is a wisdom analogue to 'a cup of cold water... he will in no way lose his reward' (10:42), though the proverb concerns an enemy. Thematic and disputed.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Abraham climbed the mountain with his only son.
How long, O Lord? Will you forget us?
He looked up, and God had provided the lamb.
The Lord will provide; we trust your steadfast love.
Whoever gives a cup of cold water has not lost the reward.
Even the smallest welcome is seen.
Come, let us worship the God who provides.
We come, and we trust. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel a cup of cold water pressed into your hand on the hottest day — small, ordinary, and enough to save you.
The Lord will provide.
Abraham went up the mountain with the knife and the fire and no lamb, asking the question every aching heart asks.
The Lord will provide.
And there in the thicket, caught by its horns, was the lamb God had set aside all along.
The Lord will provide.
Jesus says even a cup of cold water given in his name is counted — so come, give and receive the smallest mercy.
The Lord will provide. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Abraham climbed the mountain, the question on his lips.
The Lord will provide.
And there in the thicket was the lamb.
The Lord will provide.
A cup of cold water, given in his name, is counted.
The Lord will provide.
Come, let us worship the God who supplies our need.
The Lord will provide. Amen.
